opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so explaining an individual response is really just the starting point. When we trace a single prompt, say, how the model does a bit of two-step reasoning or plans a rhyme ahead of time, we get a snapshot of the mechanism for that one input. That's useful, but what I'm most excited about is moving from those case studies toward something more general.

One piece is understanding the recurring building blocks: which features and circuits show up again and again across very different prompts. If the same internal representation of, say, a geographic fact or an arithmetic operation gets reused in many contexts, that tells you something about how the model actually organizes its knowledge rather than how it handled one example.

Another piece is understanding behaviors at a higher level, things like when the model is being faithful in its stated reasoning versus kind of working backward from an answer it already wants to give, or what's actually happening internally when it hallucinates versus when it correctly says "I don't know." Those are questions about patterns of behavior, and answering them means looking across many examples and finding the shared mechanisms.

And ultimately, the longer-term goal is something closer to a map of the model: being able to say, here are the major capabilities, here's roughly how they're implemented, and here's how they interact. We're far from that today. Our tools still only capture a fraction of what's going on, and there's a lot of what we sometimes call dark matter we can't yet see. But the hope is that by accumulating these individual explanations and building better tools, we can get to a point where we can reason about the model's behavior in general, including in situations we haven't explicitly tested, which matters a lot for both science and safety.

r001.rationale: The response says the goal is to move beyond individual case studies toward shared mechanisms and a broader map of Claude’s capabilities and behavior, including situations not explicitly tested.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so explaining individual responses is really valuable, and that's a big part of what we do. You take a specific prompt, you trace how the model got from the input to the output, and you learn something about the mechanism behind that one behavior. But the thing I keep coming back to is that a single explanation is kind of like a single case study. It tells you what happened in that instance, and it doesn't necessarily tell you how the model behaves in general.

So one direction I'm really interested in is moving from explanations of individual outputs to something more like a characterization of the model as a whole. What are the recurring circuits, the recurring strategies that show up across many different prompts? If you look at how Claude plans ahead in a poem, or how it does multi-step reasoning when answering a factual question, do those same pieces show up when it's writing code, or when it's being asked a safety-relevant question? That's much closer to the kind of understanding you'd want if you actually want to make claims about the system, rather than claims about a particular response.

Another piece of it is understanding the model's representation of itself and of the situation it's in. We've seen features that seem to correspond to the model's sense of what it is, whether it's being tested, what kind of entity it's talking to. Those are interesting because they're not really about any one output. They're more like a persistent state that then shapes a lot of outputs downstream. So being able to say, here's how the model represents its own goals, or here's how it represents the user, and here's how that influences behavior, that feels like a different kind of question than "why did it say this word."

And then the third thing, which is maybe the most ambitious, is getting to a point where the understanding is predictive rather than just descriptive. Right now a lot of interpretability is retrospective. The model did something, and we go in and figure out why. What I'd love is to be able to look at the internals and say, in advance, this model is going to have trouble with this class of problems, or this model has learned a shortcut here that's going to break under distribution shift. That's the kind of understanding that would actually let you catch issues before they show up in deployment, which is really the goal of all this.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts single-response explanations with characterizing Claude as a whole, identifying recurring circuits and strategies across many prompts as a goal.

astra-6.text:
I’m interested in understanding Claude at the level of the model, rather than just understanding why it gave a particular answer. What concepts has it learned? How does it represent those concepts, and how does it use them across different situations?

An explanation of one response can be useful, but I’d like to get to an understanding that lets us make predictions. If we think we’ve identified a mechanism, can we predict when it will show up in a different context? And if we intervene on it, does the model’s behavior change in the way we expect? That would give us a much stronger basis for saying we understand something about how Claude works.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts explaining one answer with understanding Claude’s model-level concepts and mechanisms across different situations, including predicting when they appear.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m interested in understanding Claude at the level of its internal mechanisms. Explaining why it gave one particular answer is useful, but I’d also like to know what concepts it represents, how those concepts interact, and how it uses them across different situations. Are we seeing the same underlying computation in two tasks that look very different on the surface?

The goal is to build an understanding that lets us make predictions. If we think we’ve identified a mechanism, can we predict when it will activate, or how changing it will affect the model’s behavior? That would give us something more useful than a plausible story about an individual response.

r001.rationale: The response goes beyond explaining one answer by seeking internal mechanisms and concepts that recur across different situations, including whether different-looking tasks use the same computation.
